title: OpenAI releases ChatGPT
summary: A free research preview of a conversational model reaches the public. The release turns general-purpose AI from a research and policy question into a mass-market product and a subject of national competition.
why: No instrument was adopted. The governance response that followed — summit declarations, codes, the EU AI Act's final negotiations and the AI-specific treaties — was driven by the public salience this release created. The legal record begins after the market event, not before it.

title: United States and India launch the iCET
summary: The inaugural meeting of the US–India Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology is held in Washington. The fact sheet covers AI, semiconductors, quantum, advanced telecommunications and defence innovation, and announces work on common standards and benchmarks for trustworthy AI.
why: A bilateral technology arrangement with no treaty, depositary or ratification. It is one of the earliest US attempts to align AI standards with a partner outside the G7, and it shows how much AI cooperation happens outside the legal instruments in the catalogue.

source.label: US Embassy in India, iCET fact sheet

title: Biden–Xi summit at Woodside: AI talks and military channels
summary: The two presidents meet in Woodside, California. They affirm the need to address the risks of advanced AI through government talks, and welcome the resumption of high-level military-to-military communication, including telephone conversations between theater commanders.
why: The summit produced no document and no legal instrument. It created a political channel: the AI dialogue that met in Geneva in 2024, and the military telephone links that are a hotline in all but name. Neither appears in a treaty or a declaration.

title: First US–China intergovernmental dialogue on AI, Geneva
summary: Delegations from the White House, State Department and Commerce meet Chinese counterparts from the Foreign Ministry, Science and Technology, the NDRC, the Cyberspace Administration and MIIT. They exchange views on AI risk and safety. No joint statement or deliverable is issued.
why: The meeting implements the Woodside understanding without creating an instrument. It is the clearest example of AI risk management conducted through a bilateral channel that has no legal form, no secretariat and no published rules.

source.label: US Mission Geneva, statement of 15 May 2024

title: Biden–Xi meeting in Lima: human control over nuclear weapons
summary: The leaders affirm that human beings, not AI, must make the decision to use nuclear weapons, and stress the need to develop military AI prudently and responsibly. The understanding is recorded in readouts, not in a signed text.
why: A verbal understanding between two nuclear powers on the most consequential AI red line. It creates no legal obligation, no verification mechanism and no treaty. Its importance is precisely that it is political and reversible.

title: DeepSeek releases R1
summary: A Chinese lab releases a reasoning model under the MIT licence, with open weights and a technical report, claiming performance comparable to a leading US model at a fraction of the cost. The release moves the cost of frontier capability and the open-weights question to the centre of the policy debate.
why: No instrument. The episode changed the premises of export-control and compute policy and exposed how quickly market events outrun the treaty calendar. It is part of the explanation for the supply-chain turn visible in Pax Silica and the San Francisco Declaration.

title: Stargate announced at the White House
summary: OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle and MGX announce a new company intended to invest up to $500 billion over four years in AI infrastructure in the United States, starting with data centres in Texas.
why: A private infrastructure project announced as a strategic capability. It has no legal form in international law, but it sets the compute baseline against which export controls, supply-chain coalitions and the security framing of the San Francisco Declaration are measured.

title: UN GGE adopts the 2015 cyber-norms report
summary: The UN Group of Governmental Experts reaches consensus on report A/70/174: international law applies to State conduct in cyberspace, and a set of voluntary norms, rules and principles of responsible State behaviour is set out.
why: No treaty and no supporter list. The report became the common reference for later political texts: the Paris Call, the Pall Mall Code and national cyber strategies reuse its norms language. It explains why non-binding cyber instruments cluster around the GGE vocabulary rather than around a single convention.

title: WannaCry ransomware attack
summary: WannaCry encrypts computers in hospitals, companies and public services across many countries. The UK National Audit Office later finds that the NHS was warned about the risk and that patching and contingency planning were inadequate.
why: No instrument. The attack made ransomware and unpatched critical infrastructure a leaders' issue and fed the later turn to incident response, supply-chain security and national cyber strategies. It is part of the reason cyber instruments after 2017 focus on critical activities rather than only on criminal procedure.

source.label: UK National Audit Office, WannaCry investigation

title: SolarWinds supply-chain compromise disclosed
summary: CISA releases Emergency Directive 21-01 after the SolarWinds Orion code compromise. The incident affects US government agencies and private companies through a trusted software supply chain.
why: No instrument. It moved supply-chain security and software integrity to the centre of cyber policy and is part of the background to the OECD critical-activities recommendation, the EU Cyber Resilience Act and later state-level codes.

source.label: CISA, Emergency Directive 21-01 and SolarWinds advisory

title: Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack
summary: A ransomware attack forces Colonial Pipeline to shut down a major US fuel pipeline. CISA and the FBI issue a joint advisory on DarkSide ransomware and critical-infrastructure disruption.
why: No instrument. The disruption showed that ransomware against critical infrastructure is a national-security and continuity problem, not only a crime. It is part of the context for the International Counter Ransomware Initiative and for the critical-infrastructure focus of later cyber instruments.
